source: Durian Orchard (ការដាំធូរេន), by Vann Thana Busab and Montry Vong Phanith, published by the Northwest Cambodia Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (Battambang), 1998, 59pp, AIDOC code 178-001
text:
This source illustrates four traditional durian fruit types with hand-drawn diagrams of the whole fruit and a cut cross-section, each labeled with a name and each given a bullet list of strengths (គុណសម្បត្តិ) and weaknesses (គុណវិបត្តិ) that a grower would look for when judging fruit quality by eye. The four labels, transcribed as best as the scanned handwritten-style print allowed, are: ពូជអាកនី (Aak Ni type), ពូជម៉្នចង (Mon Chong / Man Chong type), ពូជកានយ៉ារ (Kan Yiar / Kan Yav type, long-stalked), and ពូជក្រាក់ខុម (Krak Khom type).

Across the four entries, the kinds of traits listed as strengths include: thick, well-filled flesh with a good ratio of flesh to seed; small, thin, or non-viable seeds; firm flesh that holds together well without turning mushy and keeps well after ripening; good flavor and attractive flesh color; and reliable, heavy flowering and fruit-set. Traits listed as weaknesses for other types include: flowers that open but set fruit poorly; branches prone to breaking under fruit load; susceptibility to leaf and stem disease; and fruit prone to splitting at the stalk or base.

Because the source page images available for this batch were a hand-drawn, low-contrast scan, the individual line-by-line strengths and weaknesses could not be matched to each of the four specific type names with full confidence, so they are reported here as the general pool of criteria used across the four entries rather than attributed type-by-type. A grower wanting the precise strengths/weaknesses listed for one specific named type should have this page re-checked against a clean copy of the source, and the Romanized spelling of all four names should be verified with a local agricultural officer before use in formal variety recommendations.
